question: A patient asks when fingerprints and fingernails begin forming during development. Which gestational age range best matches this milestone?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Gestational weeks nine through twelve
options.rationale: Lecture states fingerprints and fingernails form during gestational age 9–12 weeks; this directly matches the milestone.

options.text: Gestational weeks four through eight
options.rationale: Weeks 4–8 involve early organogenesis (brain, heart, limbs); fingerprints/fingernails form later in 9–12 weeks; it would be correct if lecture placed nail formation earlier.

options.text: Gestational weeks fourteen through sixteen
options.rationale: Weeks 14–16 include toenail appearance and ossification; not fingernail fingerprint formation; would be correct if the slide listed fingernails at 14–16 weeks.

options.text: Gestational weeks twenty one through twenty four
options.rationale: Weeks 21–24 focus on vernix, brown fat, and surfactant onset; not initial fingerprint formation; would be correct if fingerprints developed in the second trimester.

options.text: Gestational weeks thirty three through thirty six
options.rationale: Weeks 33–36 involve fat deposition and grasp reflex; fingerprints form much earlier; would be correct only if the lecture shifted nail development to late third trimester.

question: Which definition correctly distinguishes gestational age from embryonic (postconceptional) age?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the difference between gestational age and embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Gestational age counts from first day of last menstrual period
options.rationale: Lecture defines gestational age as calculated from the first day of the LMP, whereas embryonic age is from fertilization; this matches the slide definition.

options.text: Gestational age counts from estimated day of fertilization
options.rationale: This describes embryonic (postconceptional) age, not gestational age; it would be correct if the terms were reversed in the lecture.

options.text: Embryonic age equals gestational age plus two weeks
options.rationale: Lecture states gestational age = embryonic age + 2 weeks, so embryonic age is gestational minus two weeks; this option is the inverse and thus incorrect.

options.text: Embryonic age counts from first missed menstrual period
options.rationale: Missed menses relates to gestational dating by LMP, not embryonic age; would be correct only if embryonic age were tied to menstrual timing in the lecture.

options.text: Gestational age is measured only after ultrasound confirmation
options.rationale: Ultrasound can confirm or redates gestational age but gestational age is defined from LMP; this would be correct only if the lecture redefined gestational age exclusively by ultrasound.

question: A clinician wants to calculate an estimated due date (EDD) for a patient with a known LMP. Which method matches the lecture's recommended calculation?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: Add 280 days to first day of last menstrual period
options.rationale: Lecture states EDD is 40 weeks after first day of LMP, equivalent to adding 280 days; this is the recommended calculation.

options.text: Add 266 days to first day of last menstrual period
options.rationale: Adding 266 days is used when date of conception is known, not when using LMP; would be correct only if conception date were used.

options.text: Subtract two weeks from gestational age then add 280 days
options.rationale: This misapplies the embryonic/gestational offset; correct method is simply add 280 days to LMP; would be correct only if gestational age were defined differently.

options.text: Use ultrasound dating exclusively regardless of LMP
options.rationale: Lecture recommends ultrasound-established dates take precedence when discrepancies exist but does not state ultrasound should always replace LMP; would be correct only if ultrasound were mandated.

options.text: Add 300 days to first day of last menstrual period
options.rationale: Adding 300 days is not in the lecture and would overestimate gestation; would be correct only if the lecture used a different calendar convention.

question: Which fetal structure measurement is most accurate for dating pregnancy in the first trimester according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: Crown rump length measurement
options.rationale: Lecture states first-trimester ultrasound using CRL is the most accurate method to establish or confirm gestational age.

options.text: Biparietal diameter measurement
options.rationale: BPD is used later (second trimester onward) for dating; would be correct only if the lecture recommended BPD in the first trimester.

options.text: Abdominal circumference measurement
options.rationale: AC is used for estimating fetal weight and later dating, not first-trimester dating; would be correct only if AC were validated for early gestation.

options.text: Femur length measurement
options.rationale: FL is part of second-trimester biometric measures; would be correct only if FL were accurate in the first trimester per lecture.

options.text: Head circumference measurement
options.rationale: HC is used in later ultrasound dating, not the most accurate first-trimester measure; would be correct only if lecture prioritized HC early.

question: Which fetal milestone is expected by gestational weeks 14–16 per the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Appearance of fetal toenails
options.rationale: Lecture lists toenail appearance as a feature of gestational age 14–16 weeks.

options.text: Onset of surfactant secretion by type II cells
options.rationale: Surfactant secretion begins later (type II pneumocytes start secreting around 21–24 weeks); would be correct only if the lecture shifted surfactant onset earlier.

options.text: Physiological midgut herniation returning to abdomen
options.rationale: Midgut herniation returns by about 12 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if the lecture delayed return to 14–16 weeks.

options.text: Formation of fingerprints and fingernails
options.rationale: Fingerprints and fingernails form at 9–12 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if those milestones were reallocated to 14–16 weeks.

options.text: Differentiation of ovaries with primordial follicles
options.rationale: Ovarian differentiation with primordial follicles is noted around 14–16 weeks but the lecture specifically pairs toenails with 14–16; this option would be correct if the slide emphasized ovarian timing instead.

question: A pregnant patient at 18 weeks asks whether fetal respiration is possible now. Based on the lecture, which statement is most accurate?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Respiration is not possible; no alveoli present
options.rationale: Lecture states during 17–20 weeks the canalicular period begins and no alveoli are present, so respiration is not possible.

options.text: Respiration is fully possible with mature alveoli
options.rationale: Alveoli mature much later; would be correct only if lecture indicated alveolar development by 17–20 weeks.

options.text: Respiration possible due to surfactant secretion
options.rationale: Type II pneumocytes begin secreting surfactant around 21–24 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if surfactant began earlier.

options.text: Respiration possible because lungs complete development
options.rationale: Lung development completes near term; would be correct only if lecture stated lung maturity by midsecond trimester.

options.text: Respiration possible due to fetal breathing movements
options.rationale: Fetal breathing movements may occur but effective respiration requires alveoli and surfactant; would be correct only if alveolar structures were present.

question: Which feature is characteristic of gestational weeks 21–24 according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Skin covered with vernix caseosa
options.rationale: Lecture lists vernix caseosa covering the skin as a feature of 21–24 weeks.

options.text: Formation of eyelashes and pupillary reflex
options.rationale: Eyelashes and pupillary reflex are noted later (29–32 weeks); would be correct only if lecture placed these earlier.

options.text: Testicular descent into scrotum completed
options.rationale: Testicular descent occurs around 29–32 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if descent timing were earlier.

options.text: Firm grasp reflex and muscle development
options.rationale: Firm grasp and muscle/fat deposition are features of 33–36 weeks; would be correct only if grasp developed earlier.

options.text: Circulatory system finishes development
options.rationale: Circulatory completion is near term (37–40 weeks); would be correct only if the lecture indicated earlier completion.

question: Which lung development stage begins around 17–20 weeks as described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Canalicular period of lung development
options.rationale: Lecture explicitly states the canalicular period begins during 17–20 weeks.

options.text: Pseudoglandular stage of lung development
options.rationale: Pseudoglandular stage occurs earlier (first trimester) per lecture; would be correct only if stages were reordered.

options.text: Terminal saccular stage of lung development
options.rationale: Terminal saccular stage starts later (around 25–28 weeks) per lecture; would be correct only if saccular stage began earlier.

options.text: Alveolar multiplication stage
options.rationale: Alveolar stage occurs late in gestation and postnatally; would be correct only if alveoli formed by 17–20 weeks.

options.text: Surfactant-independent lung maturation stage
options.rationale: Lecture emphasizes surfactant production begins later; this named stage is not in the lecture and would be correct only if surfactant were irrelevant.

question: Which prenatal test is described in the lecture as diagnostic and performed between 10.5 and 12.5 weeks?
cited_learning_objective: List and explain the basic procedures for assessing fetal status (II, 1)

options.text: Chorionic villus sampling diagnostic procedure
options.rationale: Lecture states CVS is done between 10.5 and 12.5 weeks, is invasive, and diagnostic for chromosome number.

options.text: Noninvasive prenatal testing using cell free DNA
options.rationale: NIPT is noninvasive and can be done at 10 weeks but is a screening test, not diagnostic; would be correct only if NIPT were diagnostic.

options.text: Second trimester quad screen maternal blood test
options.rationale: Quad screen is a second-trimester screening test, not performed at 10.5–12.5 weeks; would be correct only if quad screen timing were earlier.

options.text: Amniocentesis performed between ten and twelve weeks
options.rationale: Amniocentesis is typically done in the second trimester and is diagnostic; would be correct only if lecture recommended earlier amniocentesis.

options.text: First trimester nuchal translucency ultrasound only
options.rationale: Nuchal translucency is part of first-trimester screening but is not an invasive diagnostic test like CVS; would be correct only if the question asked about screening.

question: Which component is NOT part of the quad screen described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: List and explain the basic procedures for assessing fetal status (II, 1)

options.text: Alpha fetoprotein is part of the quad screen
options.rationale: AFP is included in the quad screen; this option is incorrect because AFP is indeed a component.

options.text: hCG is part of the quad screen
options.rationale: hCG is included in the quad screen; this option is incorrect because hCG is a component.

options.text: Estriol is part of the quad screen
options.rationale: Estriol is included in the quad screen; this option is incorrect because estriol is a component.

options.text: Inhibin-A is part of the quad screen
options.rationale: Inhibin-A is included in the quad screen; this option is incorrect because inhibin-A is a component.

options.text: Cell free fetal DNA is part of the quad screen
options.rationale: Lecture lists cell free DNA (NIPT) separately; it is not one of the four substances in the quad screen, so this is the correct exclusion.

question: A fetus demonstrates rhythmic breathing movements and temperature control by central nervous system maturation. Which gestational age range does the lecture associate with these capabilities?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Gestational weeks twenty five through twenty eight
options.rationale: Lecture notes that by 25–28 weeks the CNS can direct rhythmic breathing and control temperature.

options.text: Gestational weeks nine through twelve
options.rationale: Weeks 9–12 involve cartilage formation and organ beginnings, not CNS-directed breathing; would be correct only if CNS maturation occurred earlier.

options.text: Gestational weeks fourteen through sixteen
options.rationale: Weeks 14–16 include toenail appearance and ossification, not mature CNS breathing control; would be correct only if lecture shifted CNS maturation earlier.

options.text: Gestational weeks thirty three through thirty six
options.rationale: 33–36 weeks involve muscle and fat deposition and grasp reflex; CNS rhythmic breathing begins earlier at 25–28 weeks per lecture.

options.text: Gestational weeks thirty seven through forty
options.rationale: Term weeks include finishing development, but CNS-directed rhythmic breathing is already present by 25–28 weeks; would be correct only if lecture delayed CNS function.

question: Which fetal monitoring method described in the lecture is noninvasive and used to assess fetal heart activity during pregnancy and labor?
cited_learning_objective: List and explain the basic procedures for assessing fetal status (II, 1)

options.text: Doppler ultrasound listening to fetal heart rate
options.rationale: Lecture mentions Doppler and ultrasonography as methods to hear the fetal heart and assess fetal well-being noninvasively.

options.text: Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling for fetal blood
options.rationale: PUBS is invasive and used for fetal blood sampling or transfusion, not routine noninvasive monitoring; would be correct only if the question asked about invasive tests.

options.text: Fetoscopy insertion of scope into uterine cavity
options.rationale: Fetoscopy is invasive for fetal procedures, not routine noninvasive heart monitoring; would be correct only if invasive visualization were requested.

options.text: Amniocentesis sampling of amniotic fluid
options.rationale: Amniocentesis is invasive and diagnostic for genetic testing, not for routine fetal heart monitoring; would be correct only if genetic diagnosis were the goal.

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of fetal structures
options.rationale: MRI is noninvasive but used for detailed structural information, not routine fetal heart rate monitoring; would be correct only if MRI were used for heart rate assessment per lecture.

question: Which statement about NIPT (noninvasive prenatal testing) is consistent with the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: List and explain the basic procedures for assessing fetal status (II, 1)

options.text: NIPT analyzes cell free fetal DNA from maternal plasma
options.rationale: Lecture describes NIPT as using cell free DNA from maternal plasma and massively parallel sequencing for aneuploidy screening.

options.text: NIPT is an invasive diagnostic test offered to all women
options.rationale: NIPT is noninvasive and a screening test, not an invasive diagnostic offered universally; would be correct only if lecture mischaracterized NIPT.

options.text: NIPT must be performed after chorionic villus sampling
options.rationale: CVS is an invasive diagnostic test performed independently; NIPT is done from maternal blood and does not require CVS; would be correct only if sequencing required CVS sample.

options.text: NIPT measures maternal serum AFP and inhibin-A
options.rationale: AFP and inhibin-A are components of the quad screen, not NIPT; would be correct only if NIPT measured these proteins.

options.text: NIPT cannot be performed before twenty weeks gestation
options.rationale: Lecture states NIPT can be done at 10 weeks; this option would be correct only if the timing were restricted to later gestation.

question: A fetus at 8 weeks gestational age shows physiological midgut herniation on ultrasound. According to the lecture, when should the intestines normally return to the abdomen?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: By about twelve weeks gestational age
options.rationale: Lecture states physiological gut herniation occurs and the intestine returns into the fetal abdomen by about 12 weeks.

options.text: By about eight weeks gestational age
options.rationale: Herniation occurs around 8 weeks and return is by 12 weeks; would be correct only if the lecture indicated immediate return at eight weeks.

options.text: By about sixteen weeks gestational age
options.rationale: Return by 16 weeks is later than lecture timing; would be correct only if the lecture delayed midgut return.

options.text: By about twenty weeks gestational age
options.rationale: Twenty weeks is well beyond the lecture's stated return time; would be correct only if abnormal persistence were described.

options.text: Midgut herniation never returns before birth
options.rationale: Lecture indicates normal return by 12 weeks; this option would be correct only if the lecture described persistent herniation as normal.

question: Which fetal tissue begins producing thyroid hormone by concentrating iodine as noted in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Fetal thyroid begins concentrating iodine and producing hormone
options.rationale: Lecture states that by 9–12 weeks the fetus begins to concentrate iodine in the thyroid and produce thyroid hormone.

options.text: Fetal pancreas begins producing insulin
options.rationale: Pancreas starts making insulin around 9–12 weeks per lecture, but the question asked specifically about thyroid hormone; would be correct only if asking about pancreas.

options.text: Fetal liver begins producing surfactant proteins
options.rationale: Liver development begins earlier but surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes in the lung, not the liver; would be correct only if lecture misattributed surfactant to liver.

options.text: Fetal kidneys begin concentrating urine
options.rationale: Kidneys begin making urine around 9–12 weeks per lecture, but they do not concentrate iodine or produce thyroid hormone; would be correct only if kidneys produced thyroid hormone.

options.text: Fetal adrenal cortex begins cortisol production
options.rationale: Adrenal maturation is not described in the lecture at 9–12 weeks; would be correct only if lecture specified early adrenal hormone production.

question: Which factor listed in the lecture is a common risk for intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)?
cited_learning_objective: List and describe the factors that influence fetal growth (II, 1)

options.text: Impaired uterine blood flow is a common risk
options.rationale: Lecture identifies impaired uterine blood flow as the most common cause of IUGR.

options.text: Maternal smoking is not associated with IUGR
options.rationale: Lecture lists smoking as a risk for IUGR; this option contradicts the lecture and would be correct only if smoking were unrelated.

options.text: Multiple gestation decreases risk of IUGR
options.rationale: Lecture lists multiples as a risk factor for IUGR, not protective; would be correct only if multiples reduced growth restriction risk.

options.text: Genetic factors never influence fetal growth
options.rationale: Lecture includes genetic factors among risks for IUGR; this option would be correct only if genetics were excluded.

options.text: Excessive maternal nutrition is the primary cause
options.rationale: Lecture does not list excessive maternal nutrition as primary IUGR cause; would be correct only if overnutrition caused growth restriction per lecture.

question: Which ultrasound-derived measurement is NOT used to calculate estimated fetal weight (EFW) per the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: Head circumference is used for EFW calculation
options.rationale: HC is listed in the lecture as one of the measurements used to calculate EFW; this option is incorrect because HC is used.

options.text: Biparietal diameter is used for EFW calculation
options.rationale: BPD is included among biometric measures for EFW per lecture; this option is incorrect because BPD is used.

options.text: Femur length is used for EFW calculation
options.rationale: FL is part of the EFW formula per lecture; this option is incorrect because FL is used.

options.text: Abdominal circumference is used for EFW calculation
options.rationale: AC is explicitly listed as used to calculate EFW in the lecture; this option is incorrect because AC is used.

options.text: Nuchal translucency is used for EFW calculation
options.rationale: Lecture lists nuchal translucency as part of first-trimester screening for aneuploidy, not as an EFW biometric, so it is not used for EFW calculation.

question: A clinician notes fetal heart activity on Doppler at 11 weeks. According to the lecture, is this finding consistent with expected timing?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: Yes; fetal heart usually audible by ten to twelve weeks
options.rationale: Lecture states the fetal heart can be heard using Doppler ultrasound by 10–12 weeks in most patients, so 11 weeks is consistent.

options.text: No; fetal heart cannot be detected before twenty weeks
options.rationale: This contradicts the lecture which indicates detection by 10–12 weeks; would be correct only if Doppler detection were much later.

options.text: Yes; fetal heart is audible only after first trimester
options.rationale: Audibility by 10–12 weeks occurs within the first trimester; this option is incorrect unless lecture delayed detection beyond the first trimester.

options.text: No; Doppler cannot detect fetal heart reliably
options.rationale: Lecture supports Doppler detection by 10–12 weeks; this option would be correct only if Doppler were unreliable per lecture.

options.text: Yes; but only with invasive fetal monitoring
options.rationale: Doppler is noninvasive per lecture; invasive monitoring is not required to hear the fetal heart at this stage; would be correct only if invasive methods were necessary.

question: Which trimester range and weeks correspond to the lecture's definition of the second trimester?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Fourteen to twenty seven weeks and six days
options.rationale: Lecture defines the second trimester as 14 0/7 to 27 6/7 weeks.

options.text: Zero to thirteen weeks and six days
options.rationale: This range corresponds to the first trimester per lecture; would be correct only if trimester boundaries were different.

options.text: Twenty eight to forty two weeks zero days
options.rationale: This range corresponds to the third trimester per lecture; would be correct only if trimester definitions were shifted.

options.text: Fourteen to thirty six weeks inclusive
options.rationale: This extends beyond the lecture's second-trimester upper limit; would be correct only if the lecture used a broader second trimester.

options.text: Twelve to twenty four weeks inclusive
options.rationale: This narrower range does not match the lecture's stated 14–27 6/7 weeks; would be correct only if the lecture used different cutoffs.

question: Which developmental event is associated with gestational weeks 29–32 in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Bone marrow becomes major site of erythropoiesis
options.rationale: Lecture indicates that by 29–32 weeks bone marrow is the major site of erythropoiesis.

options.text: Ossification of distal femoral epiphysis first appears
options.rationale: Distal femoral epiphysis ossification center is usually seen at 33 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if ossification occurred earlier.

options.text: Lanugo first appears covering the fetal body
options.rationale: Lanugo begins earlier around 17–20 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if lanugo onset were later.

options.text: External genital differentiation begins
options.rationale: External genital formation begins earlier (around 9–12 weeks) per lecture; would be correct only if genital differentiation were delayed.

options.text: Brown fat formation initiates thermogenesis
options.rationale: Brown fat forms around 21–24 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if brown fat formation were shifted to 29–32 weeks.

question: Which statement about first trimester screening between 11 and 14 weeks is accurate per the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: List and explain the basic procedures for assessing fetal status (II, 1)

options.text: Screening assesses risk for trisomy 21 and 18
options.rationale: Lecture states first-trimester screening between 11–14 weeks looks for risk (not diagnostic) of Trisomy 21 and Trisomy 18.

options.text: Screening definitively diagnoses chromosomal abnormalities
options.rationale: First-trimester tests are screening tools and not diagnostic; diagnosis requires invasive testing like CVS or amniocentesis.

options.text: Screening uses only maternal blood without ultrasound
options.rationale: Lecture specifies first-trimester screening consists of sonogram (nuchal translucency) and maternal serum tests; would be correct only if ultrasound were excluded.

options.text: Screening is performed exclusively after twenty weeks
options.rationale: Screening occurs at 11–14 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if timing were later.

options.text: Screening replaces the need for any diagnostic testing
options.rationale: Screening identifies risk and does not replace diagnostic tests; would be correct only if screening were diagnostic per lecture.

question: Which fetal characteristic is typical near term (37–40 weeks) according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Circulatory system has finished development
options.rationale: Lecture states that by 37–40 weeks the circulatory system is done developing.

options.text: Brown fat formation begins for thermoregulation
options.rationale: Brown fat forms earlier around 21–24 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if brown fat formed at term.

options.text: Physiological midgut herniation first occurs
options.rationale: Midgut herniation occurs in the first trimester and returns by 12 weeks; would be correct only if herniation began at term.

options.text: Type II pneumocytes begin initial surfactant secretion
options.rationale: Type II pneumocytes begin secreting surfactant around 21–24 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if secretion began at term.

options.text: Ovarian primordial follicles first differentiate
options.rationale: Ovarian differentiation occurs earlier (14–16 weeks) per lecture; would be correct only if differentiation were delayed to term.

question: A patient with known conception date from IVF asks how to calculate EDD. According to the lecture, which adjustment should be used?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: Add 266 days to the date of conception
options.rationale: Lecture states when date of conception is known (e.g., IVF), EDD is calculated by adding 266 days to conception date.

options.text: Add 280 days to the date of conception
options.rationale: Adding 280 days applies to LMP-based dating, not known conception; would be correct only if using LMP instead of conception date.

options.text: Subtract fourteen days then add 280 days
options.rationale: This unnecessarily adjusts LMP-based dating; would be correct only if converting between gestational and embryonic age per lecture.

options.text: Use ultrasound dating only and ignore conception date
options.rationale: Lecture notes ultrasound can confirm dates but when conception is precisely known, adding 266 days is recommended; would be correct only if ultrasound always superseded conception date.

options.text: Add 300 days to the date of conception
options.rationale: This is not in the lecture and would overestimate gestation; would be correct only if a different calendar convention were used.

question: Which invasive diagnostic test is offered after abnormal screening tests or known risk factors and can confirm chromosome number, per the lecture?

options.text: Noninvasive prenatal testing using maternal plasma

options.text: First trimester nuchal translucency ultrasound alone
options.rationale: Nuchal translucency is part of screening, not diagnostic; would be correct only if ultrasound alone were diagnostic.

options.text: Quad screen maternal serum test in first trimester

options.text: Doppler fetal heart auscultation for chromosomal diagnosis

question: Which fetal physical sign is noted in the lecture to appear during 17–20 weeks and later cover the body?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Lanugo, soft downy hair covering the body
options.rationale: Lecture states lanugo starts to form and cover the body during 17–20 weeks.

options.text: Vernix caseosa covering the skin

options.text: Firm grasp reflex development
options.rationale: Firm grasp is described at 33–36 weeks; would be correct only if grasp developed earlier.

options.text: Distal femoral epiphysis ossification center visible
options.rationale: Distal femoral epiphysis ossification center is usually seen at 33 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if ossification occurred earlier.

options.text: Testicular descent into scrotum completed
options.rationale: Testicular descent is noted around 29–32 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if descent occurred earlier.

question: Which statement about redating pregnancy by ultrasound does the lecture recommend for first-trimester scans?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: Redate if ultrasound differs from LMP by more than five days
options.rationale: Lecture's table indicates for ≤8 6/7 wk (first trimester) a discrepancy of more than 5 days supports redating by ultrasound.

options.text: Redate only if ultrasound differs by more than twenty one days
options.rationale: Twenty-one days applies to third-trimester discrepancies per lecture, not first trimester; would be correct only if using third-trimester criteria.

options.text: Never redate pregnancy based on ultrasound

options.text: Redate if ultrasound differs by more than fourteen days in first trimester

options.text: Redate only when LMP is unknown regardless of ultrasound
options.rationale: Lecture uses both LMP and ultrasound and provides thresholds for redating; would be correct only if ultrasound were ignored when LMP known.

question: Which fetal organ begins making urine by 9–12 weeks as noted in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Kidneys begin producing fetal urine
options.rationale: Lecture states kidneys begin making urine during 9–12 weeks gestational age.

options.text: Liver begins producing bile for digestion
options.rationale: Lecture mentions liver development begins but not bile production at 9–12 weeks; would be correct only if bile production were specified.

options.text: Pancreas begins producing surfactant proteins
options.rationale: Pancreas starts making insulin per lecture, not surfactant; surfactant is produced by lung type II pneumocytes.

options.text: Thyroid ceases iodine concentration
options.rationale: Lecture indicates the fetal thyroid begins concentrating iodine and producing hormone, not ceasing it; would be correct only if thyroid function were suppressed.

options.text: Lungs begin alveolar gas exchange
options.rationale: Alveoli are not present at 17–20 weeks and gas exchange is not possible until later; would be correct only if alveoli were present early.

question: Which procedure listed in the lecture provides definitive chromosome number information and is invasive?
cited_learning_objective: List and explain the basic procedures for assessing fetal status (II, 1)

options.text: Chorionic villus sampling provides definitive karyotype
options.rationale: Lecture describes CVS as invasive, diagnostic, and tells number of chromosomes.

options.text: Noninvasive prenatal testing provides definitive karyotype
options.rationale: NIPT is screening using cell free DNA and is not diagnostic; would be correct only if NIPT were diagnostic per lecture.

options.text: Quad screen provides definitive chromosomal diagnosis
options.rationale: Quad screen gives risk estimates and is not diagnostic; would be correct only if quad screen were diagnostic.

options.text: Ultrasound anatomy scan provides definitive karyotype
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses anatomy and anomalies but cannot definitively determine chromosome number; would be correct only if ultrasound could read chromosomes.

options.text: Doppler fetal heart auscultation provides definitive karyotype
options.rationale: Doppler assesses heart rate and cannot diagnose chromosomal abnormalities; would be correct only if heart sounds correlated with karyotype.

question: Which fetal feature is specifically noted in the lecture to protect skin and have anti-infective properties around midsecond trimester?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Vernix caseosa acts as protective skin film
options.rationale: Lecture describes vernix caseosa as a waxy substance protecting skin with anti-infective and waterproofing properties.

options.text: Lanugo provides waterproofing and infection protection
options.rationale: Lanugo is soft hair and not described as anti-infective or waterproofing; would be correct only if lecture attributed those properties to lanugo.

options.text: Brown fat provides skin protection and waterproofing
options.rationale: Brown fat is for thermogenesis, not skin protection; would be correct only if brown fat had protective skin functions per lecture.

options.text: Amniotic fluid forms a waxy protective film
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid surrounds the fetus but lecture attributes waxy protective film specifically to vernix; would be correct only if amniotic fluid were described that way.

options.text: Fetal epidermis secretes surfactant for protection
options.rationale: Surfactant is secreted by type II pneumocytes in lungs, not by epidermis; would be correct only if epidermis produced surfactant per lecture.

question: Which timing and test pairing from the lecture is correct for first-trimester diagnostic sampling?
cited_learning_objective: List and explain the basic procedures for assessing fetal status (II, 1)

options.text: CVS between ten and twelve and a half weeks
options.rationale: Lecture specifies chorionic villus sampling is done between 10 1/2 and 12 1/2 weeks and is diagnostic.

options.text: Amniocentesis between ten and twelve and a half weeks
options.rationale: Amniocentesis is typically performed later (second trimester) per lecture; would be correct only if early amniocentesis timing were endorsed.

options.text: NIPT only after twenty weeks gestation
options.rationale: Lecture states NIPT can be done at 10 weeks; would be correct only if NIPT timing were restricted to later gestation.

options.text: Quad screen performed between eleven and fourteen weeks
options.rationale: Quad screen is a second-trimester test per lecture; would be correct only if quad screen were moved earlier.

options.text: Anatomy ultrasound performed before ten weeks gestation
options.rationale: Anatomy scan is typically done between 16–22 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if anatomy scan were earlier.

question: Which fetal biometric parameter is paired with the anatomical landmark falx cerebri on ultrasound as shown in the lecture schematic?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: Biparietal diameter uses falx cerebri landmarks
options.rationale: Lecture schematic shows BPD with landmarks including the falx cerebri, cavum septum pellucidum, and thalamus.

options.text: Abdominal circumference uses falx cerebri landmarks
options.rationale: AC uses abdominal landmarks (umbilical vein, stomach, spine), not falx cerebri; would be correct only if AC used cranial landmarks.

options.text: Femur length uses falx cerebri landmarks
options.rationale: FL uses femur landmarks (trochanter), not cranial structures; would be correct only if FL used head landmarks.

options.text: Head circumference uses umbilical vein landmarks
options.rationale: HC uses cranial landmarks, not the umbilical vein; would be correct only if HC used abdominal structures.

options.text: Nuchal translucency uses femur trochanter landmarks
options.rationale: Nuchal translucency is a neck measurement and does not use femur trochanter landmarks; would be correct only if NT used femoral landmarks.

question: Which gestational age range in the lecture is associated with the beginning of ossification of the fetal skeleton?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Fourteen to sixteen weeks ossification begins
options.rationale: Lecture lists ossification of the fetal skeleton as occurring around 14–16 weeks.

options.text: Nine to twelve weeks ossification begins
options.rationale: 9–12 weeks involve cartilage formation and bone cell replacement but lecture specifies ossification timing at 14–16 weeks; would be correct only if ossification started earlier.

options.text: Twenty one to twenty four weeks ossification begins
options.rationale: 21–24 weeks focus on vernix and brown fat; ossification begins earlier per lecture; would be correct only if ossification were delayed.

options.text: Thirty three to thirty six weeks ossification begins
options.rationale: 33–36 weeks show distal femoral epiphysis ossification center visibility, not initial ossification; would be correct only if ossification began very late.

options.text: Thirty seven to forty weeks ossification begins
options.rationale: By term ossification is advanced; initial ossification is earlier per lecture; would be correct only if ossification onset were at term.

question: Which fetal reflex or behavior is noted in the lecture to develop by 21–24 weeks?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Suck reflex development occurs by twenty one to twenty four weeks
options.rationale: Lecture states the suck reflex is developing during 21–24 weeks.

options.text: Firm grasp reflex develops by twenty one to twenty four weeks
options.rationale: Firm grasp is described at 33–36 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if grasp developed earlier.

options.text: Pupillary reflex develops by twenty one to twenty four weeks
options.rationale: Pupillary reflex is noted at 29–32 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if pupillary reflex occurred earlier.

options.text: Rhythmic breathing directed by CNS begins by twenty one to twenty four weeks
options.rationale: CNS-directed rhythmic breathing is noted at 25–28 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if it began earlier.

options.text: Voluntary grasp and purposeful movement by twenty one to twenty four weeks
options.rationale: Purposeful grasp develops later (33–36 weeks); would be correct only if voluntary grasp appeared earlier.

question: Which statement about fetal alcohol spectrum features does the lecture explicitly note?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Only ten to fifteen percent with FASD show classic facial features
options.rationale: Lecture notes that only 10–15% of people with FASD have the characteristic facial features, highlighting variability in presentation.

options.text: All infants exposed to alcohol show the classic facial features
options.rationale: This contradicts the lecture which states only 10–15% show facial features; would be correct only if lecture claimed universal facial findings.

options.text: Facial features are the most sensitive indicator of FASD
options.rationale: Lecture implies facial features are uncommon and not the most sensitive indicator; would be correct only if facial features were highly sensitive.

options.text: FASD facial features always predict neurodevelopmental outcome
options.rationale: Lecture does not state facial features reliably predict neurodevelopment; would be correct only if lecture linked facial features to outcomes.

options.text: No infants in North Carolina continue alcohol use during pregnancy
options.rationale: Lecture provides statistics showing some women continue drinking during pregnancy; would be correct only if the lecture reported zero continued use.

question: A neonate is born with long fingernails, dry peeling skin, and loss of subcutaneous fat. Based on the lecture, which gestational timing is most consistent with this presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Postterm infant born after forty two weeks gestation
options.rationale: Lecture states postterm (42+ weeks) infants are more likely to have loss of subcutaneous fat, long fingernails, and dry peeling skin.

options.text: Preterm infant born before thirty seven weeks gestation
options.rationale: Preterm infants typically have less fat and immature skin but the lecture specifically associates long nails and peeling skin with postterm; would be correct only if lecture linked these signs to prematurity.

options.text: Term infant born between thirty nine and forty weeks gestation
options.rationale: Term infants usually have mature fat stores and skin; would be correct only if lecture described these features at term.

options.text: Late preterm infant born between thirty four and thirty six weeks
options.rationale: Late preterm infants may have immature features but the lecture highlights postterm changes for long nails and peeling skin; would be correct only if lecture associated them with late preterm.

options.text: Early term infant born between thirty seven and thirty eight weeks
options.rationale: Early term infants are not described in the lecture as having postterm skin and nail changes; would be correct only if lecture attributed these signs to early term.

question: A clinician suspects fetal growth restriction due to placental insufficiency. According to the lecture, which prenatal imaging or measurement would best help assess fetal size but not definitively determine gestational age?
cited_learning_objective: List and describe the factors that influence fetal growth (II, 1)

options.text: Ultrasound estimated fetal weight using biometric measures
options.rationale: Lecture emphasizes ultrasound measurements (HC, BPD, AC, FL) are used to estimate fetal weight and growth but size alone does not determine gestational age due to possible IUGR.

options.text: Maternal serum quad screen for AFP and hormones
options.rationale: Quad screen assesses risk for anomalies and aneuploidy, not direct fetal size estimation; would be correct only if quad screen measured fetal weight.

options.text: Doppler auscultation of fetal heart rate only
options.rationale: Doppler assesses heart rate and well-being but does not quantify fetal size; would be correct only if heart rate correlated with weight per lecture.

options.text: Noninvasive prenatal testing for cell free DNA
options.rationale: NIPT screens for aneuploidy using cfDNA and does not estimate fetal weight; would be correct only if cfDNA correlated with fetal size.

options.text: Chorionic villus sampling for placental histology
options.rationale: CVS is diagnostic for chromosomes and samples placenta but is invasive and not the primary tool for estimating fetal weight; would be correct only if placental histology directly estimated fetal size.

question: A 28-week fetus demonstrates eyelashes and a pupillary reflex on exam. Which gestational window in the lecture aligns with these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Twenty nine to thirty two weeks gestational age
options.rationale: Lecture notes eyelashes and pupillary reflex can be elicited around 29–32 weeks; a 28-week fetus is approaching this window and findings at 28–29 weeks are consistent.

options.text: Fourteen to sixteen weeks gestational age
options.rationale: 14–16 weeks include toenail appearance and ossification, not eyelashes and pupillary reflex; would be correct only if ocular reflexes occurred earlier.

options.text: Twenty one to twenty four weeks gestational age
options.rationale: 21–24 weeks involve vernix and brown fat formation, not pupillary reflex; would be correct only if reflexes developed earlier.

options.text: Thirty three to thirty six weeks gestational age
options.rationale: 33–36 weeks include grasp and fat deposition; eyelashes and pupillary reflex are noted earlier at 29–32 weeks per lecture; would be correct only if reflexes developed later.

options.text: Thirty seven to forty weeks gestational age
options.rationale: Term includes finishing development but eyelashes and pupillary reflex appear earlier; would be correct only if lecture delayed ocular reflexes to term.

question: A clinician is counseling a patient about redating in the second trimester. According to the lecture's table, what discrepancy threshold between ultrasound and LMP supports redating at 16 weeks gestation?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: More than seven days discrepancy supports redating
options.rationale: Lecture table indicates for 9 0/7 to 13 6/7 wk discrepancy >7 days supports redating; for 14–15 6/7 wk similar thresholds apply, so around 16 weeks a >7–10 day discrepancy is used; the lecture lists >7 days for early second trimester.

options.text: More than five days discrepancy supports redating
options.rationale: Five days is the threshold for ≤8 6/7 wk per lecture; would be correct only if applying first-trimester criteria to second trimester.

options.text: More than fourteen days discrepancy supports redating
options.rationale: Fourteen days applies to 22–27 6/7 wk per lecture, not around 16 weeks; would be correct only if using later-trimester thresholds.

options.text: Any discrepancy at all mandates redating
options.rationale: Lecture provides specific thresholds rather than redating for any discrepancy; would be correct only if the lecture required redating for any difference.

options.text: More than twenty one days discrepancy supports redating
options.rationale: Twenty-one days is the third-trimester threshold per lecture; would be correct only if applying third-trimester criteria to 16 weeks.

question: Which fetal hematopoietic shift is described in the lecture as occurring by 29–32 weeks?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the major developmental milestones of weeks 9-12, 13-16, 17-20, 21-25, 26-29, 30-34, 35-38 weeks embryological age (II, 1)

options.text: Bone marrow becomes the major site of erythropoiesis
options.rationale: Lecture states that by 29–32 weeks bone marrow is now the major site of erythropoiesis, replacing earlier hepatic production.

options.text: Liver becomes the major site of erythropoiesis
options.rationale: The fetal liver is an earlier hematopoietic site but lecture indicates bone marrow takes over by 29–32 weeks; would be correct only if liver remained primary later.

options.text: Spleen becomes the exclusive site of erythropoiesis
options.rationale: Spleen contributes earlier but is not described as the major site at 29–32 weeks; would be correct only if lecture emphasized splenic dominance.

options.text: Yolk sac resumes erythropoiesis as primary source
options.rationale: Yolk sac is an early hematopoietic site in embryogenesis, not primary at 29–32 weeks; would be correct only if yolk sac persisted as main source.

options.text: Placenta becomes the major erythropoietic organ
options.rationale: Placenta is not described as the major site of erythropoiesis in the lecture; would be correct only if placental hematopoiesis were emphasized.

question: Which clinical action aligns with the lecture when first-trimester ultrasound and LMP dates differ beyond recommended thresholds?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how to estimate the gestational age and define estimated date of confinement (II, 1)

options.text: Use ultrasound-established dates to redetermine gestational age
options.rationale: Lecture states ultrasound-established dates should take preference over menstrual dates when discrepancies exceed specified thresholds.

options.text: Always retain LMP date regardless of ultrasound findings
options.rationale: Lecture recommends redating when ultrasound and LMP differ beyond thresholds; would be correct only if ultrasound were considered unreliable.

options.text: Average the ultrasound and LMP dates for EDD
options.rationale: Lecture does not recommend averaging; it provides thresholds for when ultrasound should supersede LMP; would be correct only if averaging were endorsed.

options.text: Delay any dating decision until third trimester ultrasound
options.rationale: Lecture emphasizes first-trimester ultrasound is most accurate for dating and should be used earlier; would be correct only if early ultrasound were discouraged.

options.text: Use NIPT results to determine gestational age
options.rationale: NIPT screens for aneuploidy and does not provide gestational age dating per lecture; would be correct only if cfDNA were validated for dating.
